examples.worked_solution:
Every $n\times n$ matrix $A$ can be written in the form

$$
A = PJP^{-1},
$$

where $J$ is a Jordan canonical form (or Jordan normal form) of $A,$ and $P$ is an invertible matrix.

To find the matrix $J,$ we first find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ by solving $\det(A-\lambda I)=0{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}5-\lambda  & 4 \\ 2 & -2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (5-\lambda )(-2-\lambda )-4\cdot 2 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-3\lambda -18 & =0 \\ (\lambda -6)(\lambda +3) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, the eigenvalues are $\lambda_1=-3$ and $\lambda_2=6.$ Since we get two distinct eigenvalues, the matrix $A$ is diagonalizable, and a Jordan canonical form is

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14070655/assets/d6c87739f52f450b27c68a118bba04e51e68a377da7d0a16ae0658e1b2d547f0.png)

**Note**: A Jordan canonical form is unique up to permutations of its Jordan blocks. Therefore, another Jordan canonical form for this matrix is
